title: A Safe Size Is a Chance

scenes.tts: How many animals does a species need? In 1981, Mark Shaffer answered by changing the question. A population is never simply safe or doomed. Chance acts on it, and small populations feel that chance most.
scenes.visual: A population of dots with a question-mark size box; a safe/doomed label is crossed out and replaced by a dice for chance.
scenes.narration: How many animals does a species need? In 1981, Mark Shaffer answered by changing the question. A population is never simply safe or doomed. Chance acts on it, and small populations feel that chance most.

scenes.tts: Take an illustration. A population is down to its last breeding female, and she has five young. The chance that all five are male is one half to the fifth power. That is one in thirty two, about three percent. In a population of thousands, such luck averages out. In a population of ten, it decides the outcome.
scenes.caption: Take an illustration. A population is down to its last breeding female, and she has five young. The chance that all five are male is (1/2)^5. That is 1 in 32, about 3%. In a population of thousands, such luck averages out. In a population of ten, it decides the outcome.
scenes.visual: One female and five young drawn one by one as M or F; all five M; the product 1/2 x 5 times appears as 1/32, about 3%; then a crowd of thousands versus ten dots.

scenes.tts: So Shaffer defined a minimum viable population by a standard that someone chooses. It is the smallest isolated population, in a given habitat, with a chosen chance of persisting for a chosen time. As a tentative example, he suggested a ninety nine percent chance of lasting one thousand years. Change the chance, the time, or the habitat, and the answer changes.

Change the chance, the time, or the habitat, and the answer changes.

scenes.tts: A population viability analysis estimates that chance. Think of a weather forecast. You do not predict the future. You run it many times and report how often it rains. Here is an invented example. A hypothetical species starts with twenty individuals. The model runs one thousand times over one hundred years. In one hundred twenty runs, the population reaches zero. That is twelve percent.
scenes.caption: A population viability analysis estimates that chance. Think of a weather forecast. You do not predict the future. You run it many times and report how often it rains. Here is an invented example. A hypothetical species starts with 20 individuals. The model runs 1,000 times over 100 years. In 120 runs, the population reaches zero. That is 12%.
scenes.visual: A grid of 1,000 run cells appears; 120 turn red; the fraction 120 / 1,000 = 12.0% appears.
scenes.narration: A population viability analysis estimates that chance. Think of a weather forecast. You do not predict the future. You run it many times and report how often it rains. scenes.tts: Now start from fifty, then from one hundred. Fewer runs go extinct each time. Suppose managers choose a target of at most five percent risk in one hundred years. Twenty fails. Fifty passes. So fifty is the smallest tested size that meets the target. Sizes in between were never run, so the true threshold could lie anywhere in that range.
scenes.caption: Now start from 50, then from 100. Fewer runs go extinct each time. Suppose managers choose a target of at most 5% risk in 100 years. Twenty fails. Fifty passes. So 50 is the smallest tested size that meets the target. Sizes in between were never run, so the true threshold could lie anywhere in that range.

scenes.tts: Genetic guidelines add one more catch. Effective size is the size of an idealised population that would lose variation at the same rate. It is usually smaller than the count. Suppose fifty adults breed, ten males and forty females. Four times ten times forty, over fifty, gives thirty two. A target of one hundred then needs about one hundred sixty adults at that sex ratio. Keep this rule: a safe size is a chance over a time, and genetic guidelines count effective size, not heads.
scenes.caption: Genetic guidelines add one more catch. Effective size is the size of an idealised population that would lose variation at the same rate. It is usually smaller than the count. Suppose 50 adults breed, 10 males and 40 females. 4 × 10 × 40 / 50 gives 32. A target of 100 then needs about 160 adults at that sex ratio. Keep this rule: a safe size is a chance over a time, and genetic guidelines count effective size, not heads.
scenes.visual: Fifty adult dots (10 male, 40 female) shrink into a bar of effective size 32; the formula appears; a target bar of 100 grows a census bar to 160.
